utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic also know as Vlado.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Before we start, let me turn to Mr. Zoran Kupreskic. I will ask you to stand and let us know whether yesterday evening you were given the opportunity to enjoy fresh air for one hour in the detention unit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we did have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit. I'm very pleased that our request was complied with, and -- because, of course, this is a basic right of detainees, particularly while they are standing trial, but I had been told yesterday that repairs were underway, so it was extremely difficult. I would like, therefore, to express publicly the gratitude of the court to two persons, Mr. Edgar Hoppe, the Deputy Commanding Officer, and Mr. Christian Rohde, a legal officer in the registry, who both made it possible for the accused to enjoy one hour of fresh air. I understand in the big courtyard, in a better location than usual, and the same will apply to them this evening. Of course, as I said before, this is a basic right, but not very often it's not a privilege or a concession but very often basic rights may not be implemented because of practical difficulties. Again, let me also take the opportunity to thank Mr. Radovic for raising this issue. We may now proceed. I will turn to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we proceed to our next witness, I would like to update the Court on the recent development with a witness, and I would like to do that, if possible, in closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: (Open session) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sakib Ahmic. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. Ahmic. And for the record, could you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Sakib Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, could you tell us how old you are, or if it's easier for you, tell us what year you were born?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of January, 1933.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And in April of 1993, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: In the village of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would that be a part of a village known as Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. It is a part of Ahmici. All this comes under Ahmici, Pirici, a part of Zume, but as I was born in the village of Pirici, then I usually say Pirici, though it all belongs to Ahmici and it is, in fact, Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you live in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: You mean since my birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Pirici, and now I'm residing in the territory of Ahmici and Pirici. I have been living in the territory of Ahmici since 1957, when I built my house there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this point, may I ask the usher to show the Prosecution Exhibit next number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, you see before you an exhibit that we've called Exhibit 150. You can feel free to move that exhibit around in any way that you like in order to better familiarise yourself to what that exhibit shows. And if you look at it, can you tell us what that exhibit shows?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: This exhibit shows my area, my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you built a house in the 1950's?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And before coming to court today, I believe you had a chance to look at that map and make some circles around houses that you recognise, and that then afterward we transferred those circles through the computer so that they would look neat. Do those circles correspond or match the circles you made on the map when you looked at it before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, can you find your house on this Exhibit 150, and if so, could you point to it with the pointer that you now have in your hand and tell us what number or letter is next to that circle?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. My house has been marked with the number 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Who were some of your closest neighbours, both Croatian and Muslim, in that neighbourhood that is displayed in that Exhibit 150?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: My neighbours had their houses nearby. They were Vlatko Kupreskic here. This is his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you read out -- as you point to these houses, could you read out the letter or number that they correspond to, so we can be clear in the record?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: The letter B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you see any I other houses marked that you can identify as being your neighbours' or relatives'?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Letter L is Franjo Kupreskic's house. He is Vlatko's father. Number 56 -- 55 is Sukret Ahmic. He is next to 56. Then K is the warehouse of Vlatko Kupreskic. C is Zoran Kupreskic's house. D is Mirjan Kupreskic's house. J is Ivica Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Sukret's house. Could you tell us who Sukret is?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Sukret. Sukret is my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you give us the composition of his family, without giving any names, please?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I can. You mean his immediate family?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: He had a wife and three daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Vlatko Kupreskic's house. How long have you known Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I have known Vlatko Kupreskic since he was born. From his childhood to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And how long did you know Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Likewise. I know him from his birth to the present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And how well have you known Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Also the same. Since he was born until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea of how often through the years, and under what situations through the years you would associate with, or see Vlatko Kupreskic, Zoran Kupreskic and Mirjan Kupresic.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We would see others in passing, as neighbours. They would be working in their garden, I would be working in mine, so we would see each other more or less every day because we are the closest neighbours. We are next-door neighbours. Our houses are next to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, in 1993, were you working or were you on a retired status?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea of what you did when you were working, what your job was and where you were employed?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I was a driver of passenger vehicles. I used to drive managers. I worked in a company called Sipad Sebesic, branch office Travnik, Department Impregnacija Vitez. I was always driving passenger vehicles, driving heads of the accounting service. I even drove the Minister of Fianance of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Drago Bilandjija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And as part of your employment as a driver for the Impregnacija, did you receive regular medical examinations to determine your fitness to be a driver?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. Every year we had regular obligatory check-ups. This applied not only to me, but all of us who held responsible posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would these check-ups include eye examinations?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you recall how you did on those eye examinations?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: On the optical device, they ask you to recognise numbers and that's how they did the check-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you ever prescribed glasses?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were your eyes in good shape? Could you see well enough to be a driver for these important people?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, good eyesight, and good hearing and great care are required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, would I ask the usher at this point to show to the witness previously admitted Exhibit 138. Now, Mr. Ahmic, you described some of your neighbours, on that blow-up. Now I would like you to look at Exhibit 138 and tell us, first of all, what you see in the foreground of this photograph, the object -- the biggest object at the foreground of this photograph. Tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: My house. This is my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This is not the way your house looked in 1993, is it?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now look behind your house. Can you identify any of the houses depicted in that photograph behind your house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you look at the house that has the 1 on it first and tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: House number 1 is Mirjan Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What about house number 2?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: House number 2 is Zoran Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And house number 3?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: House number 3 is Ivica Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you identify any of the other houses not numbered?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I can. Just behind number 3 you see a roof, and that is the house of Ivo Kupreskic, Ivica's father. This one here is Jozo's house, and this one behind, his brother Ranko's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown previously entered Exhibit 139? Now, Mr. Ahmic, could you look at Exhibit 139 and see if you can identify any of the houses in this photograph? And if a house is numbered, could you refer to the number so we're clear for the record?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, I can tell you exactly that house number 1 is Mirjan Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you see any other houses that you recognise from this photograph?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can. House number 2 is Zoran Kupreskic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you see any other houses?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. I see a house, the house of Sukrija, the late Sukrija Ahmic. I see the house of Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Does the house of Vlatko Kupreskic have a number?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Vlatko Kupreskic's? Does it have a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, if you see on the photograph a number corresponding to Vlatko Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mentioned seeing the house of Sukrija. Could you point that out again using your pointer so we can see what that is?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can show it to you. This is Sukrija's house, the late Sukrija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would that be the house that appears to be near that evergreen tree in the centre of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you see your house --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: This part here is my field toilet, my outside toilet, and this is a fir tree behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can we show the next exhibit, which would be 140, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Please look at this exhibit, if you would, Mr. Ahmic, and tell us if you can identify any of the buildings in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Number 4 is the house of Vlatko Kupreskic, number 3 is the Hrustanovic house, number 2 is Sukrija Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: The first house you pointed to, you said it was number 4, and the marking on it is a little confused. Could you point to it again just so we can see which house you're referring to, using your pointer?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: You mean the house under number 4; is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, the one that looks like number 4 on that exhibit but which is, in fact, number 1.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: My apologies. It is my mistake then. But it is this house marked with 1 that is Vlatko Kupreskic's house. As I said, number 3 is Hrustanovic's house, and number 2 Sukrija Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've mentioned that some of your neighbours included Zoran, Mirjan, and Vlatko Kupreskic and that you've known them since they were born. Could you give us an idea what kind of relations you had with these three people and their families in the years before the attack in 1993? Were they good or bad?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Good relations. I had nothing bad towards them, nor did I receive anything bad from their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Over the years, did you have an opportunity to observe Zoran, Mirjan, and Vlatko grow up into young men?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. And their growing up was fine, decent, well-behaved young men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us generally what the relations were between Muslims and Croats in Ahmici in the years before the trouble in '93 and '92?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I can honestly say that they were very good relations, generally speaking, and on average, everybody was in a good relationship with everybody else, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you notice, though, that those relations tended, over time, to worsen, that there were problems? I am now trying to focus your attention on the period before the attack, in '92, '93.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I don't know. There was nothing, really. We lived well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, prior to the attack in '93, do you recall a situation that took place in Ahmici in '92 over a barricade?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it, but, frankly, I do not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall where you were during that period of time? Were you at your house in Ahmici or were you somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: To be honest, I myself cannot really tell where I was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us something a little bit about the village guard or the Territorial Defence? What do you know about that and were you part of that?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. There was the Territorial Defence which patrolled around the village at night so that nobody would bring in any extremists, or maybe set a barn on fire, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you, as a retired person, have any particular role in that Territorial Defence or village guard?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had watch duty in a school for this Territorial Defence and civilian protection, so to speak. In fact, it was civilian protection. I had a post in a school in Ahmici where we had a radio transmitter, and that is where I had my duty post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a school. Is this that elementary school building in Ahmici that is across from the mosque with the minaret?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That is that building, the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How would you describe this village guard? Was this an army or was this something else?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No, this was not an army. Let me describe it to you. It's very simple. These people were civilians who were on guard duties every night, and they had two-hour shifts on this night patrol. It was not a guard, it was a patrol. They would walk through the village from one end to the other, they would walk around, and in that sense, it was how this patrol functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I want to focus your attention to the day before the attack in 1993. Do you recall seeing anything that aroused your suspicions, or was everything perfectly quiet, as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Not everything was as usual. There were patrols in the village, and on the eve of the conflict, I went with my two sons to visit my sister who lived near Kaonik, and we were told that someone tried to get out on the main road, but the HVO apparently had put up a ramp there, so we couldn't leave. That day, sometime between 11.00 and 12.00, the three of us got into a car and went to the main road, and indeed, on the main road, I saw the HVO soldiers with rifles sitting there, and among them was Brcko Milicevic. I don't know his first name. His nickname is Brcko. And then a son of Simo Vidovic was there, then Vlatko Kupreskic was there with them and Ivo Kupreskic was there with them, and Ivo had a chair behind the school and he had a bottle of cognac in front of him. Nobody told us anything. We came down to the main road. We went to Kaonik, to my sister's, and we had no problems doing that. This is what I actually could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: In the days prior to or before the attack, did you see anything that struck you as odd or suspicious with respect to Ivica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I did see Ivica Kupreskic wearing a military uniform, and I had also heard that he was giving orders to these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you able to notice any activity around Ivica Kupreskic's house that you found interesting or suspicious?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. I remember very well. This could have been on the 13th or 14th in the evening, around 9.00. A small tonne truck, 1.5 tonne truck, came in front of the Ivica Kupreskic's house, and that evening there was no outside light that was on in front of their houses, on their houses, and it was usual that every night they had those lights on. That truck was parked there for the night, and in the morning, around 7.00, this truck left Ivica Kupreskic's yard. As it passed Zoran's house, it honked. It went onto the main road and turned off and went to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Despite these incidents, did you have any idea of what was about to happen on April 16, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I did not expect what we then experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you, at this time, tell us a little bit about your house? I believe you told us when it was built, but can you give us an idea of how big it is, or was, and how many rooms were in the house, and how many people were in the house so that we have an idea of what your house was like in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can describe it for you. This house was 8 by 9.3 metres in section. It had two rooms. On the lower part, there was a living room and a kitchen, and then we had a verandah with a small hallway and then there was a bathroom there and a small living room area and a little pantry. That was in that part of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is this a large house or a small house, or how would you describe it in terms of size?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: It's medium size, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I apologise. There was also a basement. Half of the section also had a lower level where there were two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So to be clear, the house was built on a kind of -- on a kind of a hill where part of the house had a basement and part of the house did not have a basement; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I do not understand. You mean there was a part with a basement, and what was the other part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was probably not a very good question. But if you can describe the house as being built not on a flat piece of land, but on a land that sloped downward so that there could be lower floors only on part of the house, and no lower floor on the other part of the house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There was a certain -- the terrain was sloping, it was an incline -- or decline, so we used that decline to build two additional rooms under the main level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 151.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, could you look at exhibit, what has been marked 151, and you can move it any way you want so that you can make the most sense out of it. Don't be afraid to turn it around so that it makes sense to you. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, this is more convenient for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would you tell us generally what that shows?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: This represents the foundations of the house. It represents the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you, with your pointer, take us through your house as if we were coming in through the front door and show us where the rooms are and tell us anything else of interest that you think of as you go through the house? Take us first through the front door and then show us your house, please.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: This is my house. This is the front entrance to the verandah. Here is a little bathroom and here is a pantry; three windows. The door to the living room; one window, the second window. This is the door to the room where I was staying, and this is the entrance to the second room, and there is one window and another window in the other room. So this would be my house. These are all the entrances to all the rooms (indicating). Here was a stove, around this area, here was a couch, here there was a sink, there was another couch here, here there was a little cabinet. There was a little side table with a television set. There was a table with chairs, and here was a small cot for a baby (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mentioned a baby. On April 15, 1993, the day before the attack, could you tell us who was in the house that evening beside yourself?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: On 15 April, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ahmic. The day before the attack.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: On 15 April, in the evening, we went to visit Redzib Ahmic; myself, the late Naser and his wife and the children. We stayed out till about 10.00, and thereupon we came back home and went to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was in the house when you all went to sleep that night?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: In the house, there was the late Naser, his wife, my daughter-in-law, Elvis, his stepson and their son Sejo, also deceased now, and I was in my room here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned first Naser. He was your son; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then you mentioned his wife. That would be your daughter-in-law?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then Elvis. Who was Elvis again, please?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Elvis was the son of Naser's wife. Naser's wife had been married before. She divorced and then she remarried my son Naser. Elvis is her son with her first husband who happened to be at our place. He was there for about 15 days, visiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall roughly how old Elvis was that day?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I thought he was six or seven. I always thought he was six or seven, whereas I do know about Sejad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So Elvis was essentially a young boy?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Sejo, tell us about Sejo. Who was he and about how old was he?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Sejo was the new-born baby, he was three months old, and on the morning of the Friday of the 16th of April, he was three months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How do you recall that so specifically, that on the morning of the 16th of April, he was three months old?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: You know how I know? Let me tell you. On the evening we went to Redzib Ahmic's house, he also has a male child, and he was to have the circumcision done, and on that particular night, we talked to them, and we agreed that I would go to Zenica, to the hospital there, to see when they had free time to perform the circumcision rite, and that is how I know exactly when he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 152.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, could you look at Exhibit 152 and again tell us -- move it around any way you like so that you're comfortable with it, but tell us, once you are comfortable with it, what that shows?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: On this layout, you can see the furniture that was in the rooms. Let me describe it. This is the fixed couch along the wall. This is the body of my late daughter-in-law, this is the couch on which the late Elvis slept, this is the stove, this is a chair that was there by the door, and this is the cot in which Sejo, the late Sejo slept. This is the television table, and this is a little cabinet, a cupboard (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us where you were sleeping that night, and use this diagram to display that?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I slept in this room here, in this part of the room, and it says here exactly (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, looking at the bed where Elvis slept, could you point to that again?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is Elvis's bed, the couch he slept on (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you describe that couch and tell us what that couch looked like and what kind of couch it was?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: This couch, you could pull it out to sleep on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the couch was pulled out that night to sleep on?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What kind of arms did that couch have?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: The couch had arms like this, for example, like this chair, the arms of the couch were like this. It had an arm on one side and an arm on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, were these arms in the shape of the arms on that chair; that's what you're meaning when you're saying "similar," curved like that?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Well, there was material there, they were upholstered, a lot of material on the arms. This thick. The arms were this thick with material, upholstered. That was the shape, more or less. And it had sponge inside, a foam interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention on the events of April 16, 1995 -- 1993, excuse me. Tell us where you were again that morning before the incident occurred, and use your pointer to show us.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: At that particular moment, I was here in this room, in the bed (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What is the first thing you recall happening that morning, the first thing you saw or heard that morning?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: That morning, I heard the morning call-to-prayer; and at the end of the prayer, I heard an explosion. First I heard a child who was awake, and I heard my daughter-in-law tell Naser to give him his pacifier. After that, I heard an explosion, and I jumped out of bed and went to the door. When I came to the door, I saw the light had been turned on, and I told Naser, "Turn the lights off." At that moment, when I said this, at the door, a soldier appeared. He had a black uniform on and he had black on his face, and Zoran Kupreskic entered through the door. Naser was somewhere around here, in front of the television set. He shot Naser. Mirjan had some liquid coming out of a bottle, some flam -- and the couch was set on fire. He shot at my daughter-in-law, fired at my daughter-in-law, and then went towards Elvis. At that time, I fell down and knocked my head against the wall. That was where my body was and he was standing here (indicating), and he shot at me. Through the arm of the couch, I heard a bullet, a shell falling. I went back. The child cried out. I heard the child again. And then there was shooting. They shot at the child and then left. At that moment, I got up, shot up, and went to the window. I opened the right-hand side of the window, looked through the curtains, and saw in front of Vlatko's house the Ustasha, members of the HVO. I did not dare go outside. I wanted to jump out of the window, but when I saw them, I did not dare jump out of the window to fall into their hands. So I just stayed there. I was beside myself. I saw a cable to the light bulb, I heard cries. They said, "Jure, Jure," and in my opinion, that was from Suhi Hrast, the cry came from Suhi Hrast, and he said, "Don't shoot, it's me." At that moment, I knew that it would be Gavrilo Vrebac and his brother Jure. Gavrilo, who was at the Urdelic house, and his brother, who was at Suhi Hrast's, more or less. At that moment, I knew that it must be them. I stood there, I waited for my fate. I was not able to jump out of the window. I did not dare jump through the window. The door was on fire. Part of the ceiling was on fire and fell down into the room. I could see that the window and the door had been burnt down. I looked through the window again and I saw Vlatko Kupreskic going out of the yard from the late Sukrija's yard, from the top, across my garden and in front of his own house, down towards his house. He had a coat. He was carrying something under the coat. He was carrying a coat and he had something underneath in his arms. It was a blue coat. But I stayed there for as long as I could. And as everything began to fall down from the ceiling, I had no more -- I couldn't breathe, and then I ran through the fire. I braced the fire and I reached the shed. I opened the shed, got hold of the handle, ran up by the hay. And was hay in the stable, some 70 or 80 centimetres high, all over the barn. I hid under the hay towards the wall, and that's where I hid, and that's where I watched what happened. And afterwards Flala Sukret (phoen) came out into the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Before we go on to the barn, let's go back a little bit and clarify some things about what happened in the house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us where your son Naser was when you came to the door of your bedroom, using your pointer, where he was before the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Naser was standing about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you take that marker that's next to you, and with the help of the usher perhaps, and put an X so we can identify where Naser was when you saw him before the shooting started? Make an X there so we can really see it. And where was the light switch in the house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: The light switch was here, here on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you just put a little mark next to that so we know where the light switch is? You don't need to put an X but maybe just a little dot with the marker.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: The light switch was there. We had two light bulbs in that room. One of them was on the ceiling above the table, and the second light bulb was about there, and the switches were where the dot is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you draw little circles where the light bulbs were in that room, please?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. They were about here. Hereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, I perhaps forgot to ask you this earlier and I should have asked you this earlier, but could you describe the kind of bed your daughter-in-law was sleeping on that night?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: It was not a bed, in fact, it was a mattress. No bed. The floor, and on the floor there was just a mattress, and they slept on that mattress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, on this drawing it looks like it's quite a distance from where Naser was to where the light switch is. Was it a long way in your room actually between Naser's position and the light switch?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: A metre and a half thereabouts. It's a small -- it's a small room, not a big room. Maybe a metre and a half. Maybe two metres, for example, from the switch. Two metres, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you show us again, with your pointer, where you were when you saw Naser before he was shot?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. That was where I was. I was standing here at the doorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And could you put a little mark there, perhaps a circle?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And could you tell us where the man who came into the door was when you first saw him, who you say is Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes I can. He was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The witness said that he first saw a soldier and that behind the soldier he saw Zoran Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, I can't remember, but we will check the transcript. In any case, I think the question was, "The man whom you saw."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I will certainly ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would you check, please, first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be clarified, in fact, with the witness. The witness referred to a soldier. He then referred to Zoran. He didn't say where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I will be happy to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, could you tell us where the soldier was when you first saw him enter the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It's this part when he entered the room. It was Zoran Kupreskic. Perhaps I was wrong in what I said, but -- I was wrong to use the term "soldier" instead of saying Zoran Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And could you put a mark there to show us where you first saw Zoran Kupreskic enter the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, from your position at the doorway of your room, did you have a clear and unobstructed view of the man, Zoran Kupreskic, as he entered your room -- or entered the living-room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, completely clear. No impediments. Just as we're sitting here and I can see you all. Quite clear air space. Nothing to cloud vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you look at this man's face as he entered the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: All -- I looked at him completely. I could see him all -- I could see the black where paint -- with the marker across his forehead, his nose, his face, but I could see his eyes and I knew exactly that it was Zoran Kupreskic. His forehead, his hair, it was him, my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How far away were you from him when you first saw him as he entered the room? And you can perhaps use me as a reference. If you look at me, and if you could tell us whether you were closer to him than I am to you or further away.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: A little further. About that far. Up by the table behind you, about there. The table behind you. About that far. Yes, that table. That was more or less the distance. That was the distance more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to get that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: For the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, what that distance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I believe I was standing in front of the table now occupied by Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's that in terms of metres?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm not very good in estimating metres.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: About four metres, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you say that Zoran--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we could measure in steps, measure the distance in steps so that we have a more exact notion, because we know how much a male step is, it is 75 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. This can be done maybe later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were the lights on in the room at the time you saw Zoran Kupreskic enter the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You say that Zoran Kupreskic had some black paint on his face. Could you describe what that looked like?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Across his forehead here, as if somebody had drawn a line but with a black felt-tipped pen, over his nose, as well along his chin. He made himself look like that. He was masked in that way so that you couldn't notice immediately who somebody was if they had this paint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you know immediately who this person was when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I did, immediately, from the very first time I laid eyes on him. I looked at him and I saw that it was Zoran and his brother Mirjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Let's stay with Zoran for a moment. How could you be so sure that this was Zoran when you first saw him as he came into the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: How could I not be sure. I know the child since his birth. I knew him even before he was born. I know his face, his shape, the shape of the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, tell us what you saw Zoran Kupreskic do after he entered the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Well, his rifle was aimed. When he entered the room he saw Naser, and he shot Naser immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was Naser still standing, to the best of your recollection, by the table when he was shot?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No. I apologise, but let me say this truthfully. A moment ago I described the same thing, the same situation when he entered the room and how he killed everybody in the room. And if I may say, I don't want to have to repeat this again, this incident again. I think I explained what he did and how he entered the room. If you want me to describe his entry into the room again and the killing of all of us; he entered, he was at the door, the lights were on at that moment. He saw Naser, immediately, standing up. He shot Naser down immediately. And at the same time he also shot my daughter-in-law Zehrudina, and at the same time went on to put some flammable liquid on the couch and there was a fire. He killed Elvis, at the same time, on the couch up here. I dropped down to the floor, and I knocked my head against the wall, and the lower part of my body was in front of him. He stood there and he shot at me through the arm of the couch, and luckily I was not hit. I think that the rifle butt was slightly up higher so that the bullets missed me and went behind my back. After that, they left --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, may I interrupt? I know this is quite difficult for you to talk about it, but it is important for the Tribunal to hear what happened in some detail, and we need to, I'm afraid, take you through it slowly and carefully. And I know that is difficult. If you need a rest or some time, please say so and I will request the Tribunal if they would grant that for you. We are near the lunch-hour.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No. I don't need a rest. Let us continue with our work. I don't know how clear everything has been to you from what I have said so far. Do I need to repeat anything, the same things all over again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I will need to ask you some detailed questions about what you saw in the room that day, and I will have to ask you to repeat a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're going to be going into some detail now and this may take a little while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Let us adjourn now until 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. While we are waiting for the witness, let me tell you that I have just received from Mr. Bauduin, the head of the Victims and Witnesses Unit, who has thus confirmed once again to be extremely competent and efficient, a copy of the medical report and a covering letter from Mr. Bauduin himself. I will now ask that photocopies should be made and a copy given to both parties, and then later on, we will come back to this issue. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ahmic. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ahmic. If --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. If, during the course of the afternoon, you feel the need for a rest, please let me know and I will ask the Tribunal if you can take a rest. I know this is tiring for you.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, we left off this morning at the point of going in step-by-step detail, to the best of your recollection, of what happened in your house on April 16, 1995. Just to retrace our steps a bit so we can begin, could you look at the exhibit in front of you, which is the schematic of your house, and tell us again where you were standing when you first saw Zoran Kupreskic come into the house? If you could use your pointer, please?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Here. This is it. This is where I was at the moment that Zoran Kupreskic entered (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We're just going to stay now with Zoran Kupreskic and follow him the best we can through your testimony and your recollection. Where was Zoran Kupreskic when you first saw him enter the house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Here, at the door leading to the room (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, what did you see first Zoran Kupreskic do as he entered the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: He looked around the room, he saw Naser standing, and he opened fire at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see this yourself?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I myself saw that from here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What did you see Zoran Kupreskic do after he fired at Naser, your son?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I saw him turning towards my daughter-in-law and opening fire on my daughter-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I myself saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Tell us what then did you see Zoran Kupreskic do after he fired at your daughter-in-law?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: At that moment, he headed in this direction (indicating). I fell for a moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Let me stop you there before you describe what you did. Did you remain standing in the doorway while Zoran Kupreskic shot your son Naser?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the doorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you remain standing in the doorway when you saw Zoran Kupreskic shoot at your daughter-in-law?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, after you saw Zoran Kupreskic fire at your daughter-in-law, did you see Zoran Kupreskic make any move or movement?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I saw him move towards me and Elvis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Move towards you and Elvis?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And for a moment, I lost control and fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Let's stop there for a moment. Before you lost control and fell, I want you to now backtrack just a moment and tell us whether you saw another individual enter the room that day.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At the same time, when Zoran came in, immediately after him came Mirjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you able to observe and look at Mirjan Kupreskic's face as he came into the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I looked at him in a haze because I was focusing on Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you recognise Mirjan Kupreskic when he came into the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I did. Yes, I recognised him. I'm quite sure of that. I recognised both Zoran and Mirjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell what Mirjan did as he entered the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: He poured liquid from a small bottle onto this couch here (indicating) and he set it on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were Mirjan and Zoran close together in the room so that you could observe both of them at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: At the same time came Mirjan, just after Zoran. One after the other they entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We are again on the verge of leading questions because the question was whether the two of them were close enough for the witness to be able to observe them at the same time. This means suggesting the answer to the witness to say, yes, they were close to one another. The real question would have been: Where were the two of them in the room, if I may put it that way? So I would suggest that the Prosecutor be asked to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Radovic. Yes, Mr. Moskowitz, could you please rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I believe you have already indicated, with your pointer, where Mirjan was as you observed him, but could you do that again for us so we can have an idea of his, that is Mirjan's, presence in the room, as you observed it?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. At the same time as Zoran entered the house, at the same time Mirjan followed him in, which means that Zoran, seeing Naser standing, fired at him immediately. At the same time, Mirjan was throwing or pouring this liquid over this couch and setting it on fire. So that I could easily see both of them from my vantage point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you have any doubt whatsoever that the people you saw in your house that day were Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: They were those persons, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that after Zoran shot your daughter-in-law, he made a move towards you and Elvis. Could you tell us what happened to you as Zoran came towards you?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: At that moment, I lost control and I fell and hit my head against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I can see you're pointing with the pointer, but for the record, could you tell us where you recall falling and hitting your head?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Right here (indicating), next to the couch and the wall. Right here in this corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you put a line where you fell so that we can refer to it later in the record, using that marker in front of you with the assistance of the usher?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: While you have the marker in your hand, for clarity, could you put the letter Z where Zoran was when you saw him first enter the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And could you put the letter M where you observed Mirjan Kupreskic lighting a fire?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. Here, roughly. (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you indicated you fell against or near the bed that Elvis was sleeping in. Where was your head and where were your feet?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I mark it with the marker?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think you can use the pointer and just describe.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: This is where my head was and my legs were here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So your head was near the wall and your legs were closer to the table?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, my head was right against the wall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, when you fell, I think you said you lost control. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I think that very moment I had a heart attack, that second between life and death. I don't know myself how to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you think you lost consciousness for a moment?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: For a moment, I'm sure I lost everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Once you fell, could you see anything at that point?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. I heard shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell where those shots, whether they were near you or far away from you?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Closer to me, and I could feel the casings falling on my right arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What do you remember hearing next?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I heard shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I heard the baby crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is this Sejo?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, the late Sejo. He was crying. I heard him and I heard a burst of fire after that, and then it was all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you hear the baby crying after the shots stopped?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No. I heard -- the last thing I heard was a sigh by my late daughter-in-law in that room while the house was in flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you remember doing after you heard the baby cry, then the shots, and then silence? What is the next thing you did?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I got up, I got to my feet. Once I got up, I cast a glance at late Naser, who was lying here (indicating). I saw a big pool of blood in front of his chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you go to him? Did you go to your son?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No, no. When I got to my feet, I saw Naser lying in this pool of blood around his chest, and then I went to my room, to this window (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, while you were lying behind the couch, did you get the feeling or the sense that shots were being fired at you?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely. There were shots, bursts of fire, one, two, three bursts, I could feel that they were in my direction, and I felt the casings hitting my right arm. I didn't see that, but that is what I felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How, in your view, was it possible for you not to have been struck by any of those bullets?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: My assumption is that this was because I was leaning against the couch, my head was turned this way, and so I assumed that the barrel of his rifle was not pointed accurately so that the bullets went over my back, which means -- and that is what I always thought -- that if only his barrel had been pointed further down, he would have hit me. Those are my assumptions. That was what I assumed then and later, and to this day, that is my conviction, that that is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- depicted in this photograph is a sofa or a couch.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, this is not the couch that was in your house at that time, is it?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No, no, no. That is not the couch that was in my house, but it was rather like the couch I had in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How is it similar and how is it different?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: The difference is that this couch that you see now, it is lying on the floor. The couch we had, it had legs. So that is one difference. And also my couch was a folding one. I don't know whether this one unfolds or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think you testified earlier that the couch in your house was actually folded out into a bed, and this one isn't, so that would be another difference?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question, I think. At that moment, the couch was folded out because the child was sleeping on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you look at the arm of this couch and tell us whether that was similar to the couch you had in your house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Similar, yes, it is similar to the one we had in our house. This too has an armrest like ours had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: There's a person lying there. Was that similar to the way you were lying beside the couch in April of '93?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, it's similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you explain, using this photograph perhaps to illustrate your testimony, how you believe the machine gun bullets missed you that day?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: They missed me because of the reasons I mentioned a moment ago. He was shooting through the armrest, but I assume that his rifle was tilted and the bullets went over me. If it had been lower down, it would have killed me and I wouldn't be here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you recall how Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic were dressed that morning when they were in your house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: In black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any weapons?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Who had the weapon? Zoran, Mirjan, or did they both have weapons?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I saw the weapon in Zoran's hands. I didn't really pay attention to Mirjan. I saw him come in, but I didn't pay attention to him so much. I was focusing my view on Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you focus on the kind of weapon that Zoran had?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: At that moment, I saw that it was a smaller rifle with a transparent drum with bullets inside. That is the impression I had that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Are you certain that that was the kind of rifle he had?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I'm not sure because I wasn't really looking. I wasn't interested in the weapon. I was interested in the person that I was looking at, the perpetrators who were doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that after you got up from the area near Elvis's bed, you did not go to your son's body. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I went to my room, to the window of my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I thought to myself that I should try and jump out. I opened the right-hand pane of the window and I thought I should jump out and look for a way to save my life. However, when I saw Vlatko Kupreskic in the yard, a HVO fighter, combatant, I was afraid to jump out because I thought they'd catch me alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the witness the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 154.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, could you look at the photograph placed on the ELMO machine next to you, Exhibit 154? Could you tell us what that photograph shows?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is the house -- this is my house, and here is shown the lower level, and here on the upper level there's one room and the other room. That is the windows of one and then the other rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that you re-entered your room and looked out of the window. Does this photograph show at least part of the window that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. It is this window and this part of the window, to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What does that window overlook?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: It looks over to the house of both Vlatko and Zoran Kupreskic. And I can also see Mirjan's house over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you saw when you re-entered your room and looked out of that window?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I saw a soldier in Vlatko Kupreskic's yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you then proceed to climb out of the window to make your escape, or did you remain in the room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No. When I saw the soldier there, I stayed in this room because I did not dare. I was afraid that they would see me, that they would catch me alive, and then that they would torture me, they would then burn me like they burned my entire family. That was going through my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What was going on in the rest of your house while you stood at the window and had to decide how to escape?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I heard a deep sigh of my daughter-in-law, and that was her last moment. And she was burning, she was engulfed in flames. Everything was in flames. The hall, living-room where all of them were lying, those members of my family who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you feel the heat from those flames while you were in your room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I felt tremendous heat and fire. My only -- the only thing that was helping was that the window had been open and so there was some air, but I constantly was thinking whether to jump out. But what I thought is if I jumped out and I would be killed that would be fine, but I did not want them to capture me and torture me. So what I eventually decided to do was to move from the house to the barn. And then I heard somebody shouting, "Jure, Jure." This was coming from Hrast's house, I assumed that Jure was calling back from the old oak tree which was dead, and he was saying, "Don't shoot, it's me." I assumed and I still think now that these were the two bothers, Gavrilo Verbac and his brother Jure, which means that Gavrilo was near Cico Hirica's house near my house, and that his brother was over at the Suhi Hrast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, you heard this while you were in your room?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us at what point you decided to make your escape from the house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I made the decision when I could no longer stand the heat of the flames and fire. The flames were going towards the lighting fixture, and it was as if somebody was sawing it through the ceiling. It started caving in, and the door from my room to the living-room was already burned through, and as well as the flames started coming through the window. So I could not stand that any more. I decided to run out of the house. I still had it if my mind that they may not see me. There was a Cypress tree in front of my house which blocked the view to Vlatko's house, and then I also had some construction supplies, I had cinder blocks, and that was also protecting me from view from Vlatko's house. There was also a barn there. So I managed to get to the door of the barn. I climbed up the ladder, I went to the far end of the barn, and I went and stayed against the wall of this barn or hayloft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, before we get to the barn --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- could you tell us what exit you used to leave the house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Through the flames. Through the kitchen to the veranda, the front door and in the direction of the barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Am I right then in assuming that you ran through the fire in the living-room, or in the main room in the house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: That's how I said. Maybe you didn't understand me. That's how I said. From my room I ran through the living-room where all the children were killed. I went through the living-room to the door where Zoran first appeared, and then through the veranda, main -- front door and to the barn. So I did run through the whole house. You may not have understood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you suffer any injuries by running through the fire?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: It was already in -- back in the room where I sustained burns, terrible burns, because I was there as long as I could withstand. But when it was a question of life or death, I decided to run through the fire and seek shelter up in the barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you describe for us, as best you can now, what kind of injuries and where those injuries were on your body?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I was singed all over, my head, my arms, my hands, my face. I was exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, before you made your escape from the house, while you were still in your room, I believe you told us you heard a conversation, and you also saw a HVO soldier. Do you recall seeing anything or anyone else at that time?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I heard the conversation while I was in the barn when they were letting out the livestock from the barn, the HVO soldiers did not have any conversation in the house. There was nothing except for the exchange between Zoran and Mirjan. It was when I was in the barn, when two soldiers came whom I had not seen when they entered the barn, but I just heard their conversation. He said this, when they were letting out the cows, he said, "Don't let the cows go into the garden, let them go down towards the road." So they broke the fence to my property, and they went into Vlatko Kupreskic's yard. But I really did not see who those soldiers were because they had their backs to me. So I could not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the barn.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Whose barn was that and where was that it located in relation to your house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: At the entrance to my yard, in front of the late Sukrija's house, and it was to the right when you entered my yard. So it was the right in my yard, and to the right of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would at this time ask the usher to show the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 155.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And for information for the Court, this exhibit was also taken by British soldiers on the day of the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, do you know when these photographs were taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We will have a British witness come in and give you the precise time or as best as he can estimate, but my recollection, standing here now, that it was sometime in the early afternoon, perhaps 1.00 or 2.00, maybe a little later, maybe earlier. It's not totally clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, could you look at the Exhibit 155, which is a photograph in front of you, and could you tell us what that shows?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This here shows the house of the late Sukrija Ahmic. Here is the construction supplies, the roof tiles, then the firewood. Also, chopped wood pile here. This is the barn where I was staying, and it was here where I was staying, and then farther down is the house. This is the house, part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you pointed, I think, quite briefly to where you were staying, or where you were on April 16, '93 when you left your house. Could you point again for us where you recall being on that day?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I can do it 100 per cent. I know exactly what I know. I was here exactly. This is the wall, and it was against this wall. You see that there's some netting here. This is the protective netting for the construction material. What you see red and yellow, that's the flames. I was here at this corner exactly. And you see that right at this time that the barn is still on fire. At this time I was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you describe how you placed yourself in that barn?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. When I entered the barn, I was here under the hay. I was lying there. And from there I really did have a good view both down and over to one side, the other side, everywhere. There were boards and there were cracks between boards. And from the barn -- while I was there in the barn, the soldiers arrive. They let the cows out, then they left after them. They went to Vlatko's yard. While I was in the barn (redacted). I was looking from here. He was carrying someone, but there was a stretcher. He was in front and two persons in the back, and there was a wounded person on the stretcher. They went down -- they went up to the mosque in Upper Ahmici. That was one. And then secondly, Eso Ahmic's wife passed through with three children, with a bag on her -- slung over her back, and then in the direction of Sukrija's house, this is where Sukrija was killed. She was pointing to the children to look at Sukrija as they were going up there, and then I was observing from the same position. Franjo Kupreskic came. He came out to the yard and he was letting the chickens out. And then Nikica Safradin, called Cico, arrived, and this was towards Franjo, below my house. And Franjo stopped him and said, "Go over and see what happened in Sakib's house." And I was listening to all of that from there. Cico went back to the entrance of my house. He couldn't see anything. He could just see -- just a big fire burning there. Then Cico went back to Franjo, and Franjo he said, "What did you see there?" He said in raised voice, "There's nothing. Everybody's croaked." And I'm thinking to myself not everybody's croaked. You don't know that Sakib is watching you. I was listening with my own ears, but I was not in a position to do anything there. Four or five young men came up the path while I was still there. They came(redacted) (redacted) and they went through this thicket or grove, and as they passed through there was a burst of fire and these young men were just mowed down by it. Three soldiers came out of Vlatko's house. They came to the asphalt road, to those young men over there. They looked -- they patted them over and then all three soldiers went down back towards Vlatko's house. Following that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, before you continue, let me ask a couple of clarification questions and then you may continue.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And you mentioned that he was carrying something. I wasn't all that clear on what you were saying. Could you describe what you (redacted) carrying?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Oh, that's right. Now I understood your question. First I did not understand it. I saw (redacted), from the barn, as he was walking down the road and was carrying a stretcher. He was in front and he was carrying the stretcher, and there were two persons behind him, and each of these two persons were holding one of the handles of the stretcher, and they were carrying a wounded person. I don't know who this person was. I don't even know who those two persons were in the back, but I recognised (redacted) And they went in the direction of the mosque in upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: All right. Now, you also mentioned someone pointing at Sukrija's house. First of all, could you see, from --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- your position in the barn, Sukrija's house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. It was right in front of me. Sukrija's house was right there. Sukrija's house is right next to the barn. See, this is Sukrija's house, and this is the barn in which I was. I was here at this corner. I could see everything. Of course, I could see all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you see --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I could see up front and to all sides I could see from this barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you see any bodies nearby?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Near the barn?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: From your position in the barn, looking out, near your son's home, could you see any bodies?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No. From the barn, from here, I could not see the body -- the late Sukrija's body. I didn't even know that he was lying there, that he had been killed there. It was only the following day when I was fleeing for my life that I saw him there. And I tried -- he was sort of bent, and I tried to straighten him out. But then I realised that I could not do it, and -- because I needed to save my life. I went on in the direction of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic. You indicated that you saw someone looking at or pointing at the house of Sukrija. Could you tell us who that was if you know?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know exactly. It is my nephew's Eso's wife. She came from up there by Vlatko's house, then by Sukrija and my house, and at Sukrija's house she saw the late Sukrija's body and she was pointing it to the children. She was pointing at the body to them. This is what I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At the time you saw her pointing at a body or somebody, you did not know at that time that she was looking at the body of your son, Sukrija?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No, no, I did not know what she was pointing at, what she was observing there. I did not know what she was pointing at. But later on, when I saw the dead body of Sukrija, then I put these two things together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
