utterances.text: Now, I think you also said that you saw or heard a burst of fire that appeared to strike some men. Could you tell us where that fire came from, if you can?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. When the young men came from Vlatko's house, the shot rang from that area of Vlatko's house, and those three Croat soldiers went from Vlatko's house to where those young men were killed and then later on went back to Vlatko's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you recognise any of those soldiers that came from Vlatko's house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No, no, I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What do you recall happening in addition, while you were in the barn?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Two armoured vehicles came, two tanks. They came from the main road up to Ahmici. One tank went in front of the house of Ivica Kupreskic, into his yard, and the other one came to the entrance -- to the gate of my yard, and it came to a stop here (indicating). So this tank came to a stop here. It was sitting right there, where this sand is, and I was here behind this wall. I may have been four to five metres away from it, from this tank which was standing there. When the tank came to a stop there, the turret lid opened and a soldier emerged from the tank. He looked around and went back down in. He lowered the lid. The tank, which was in Ivica Kupreskic's yard, joined him, and started in the direction of Ahmici. This tank followed it, and they went in the direction of Gornji Ahmici, Upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, while the tank was parked in front of your barn, did you give some thought to perhaps leaving the barn and going to the tank and being rescued?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I did think about that, but I wasn't 100 per cent sure that they would take me in, that they would take me into the tank, and so I was afraid that they wouldn't take me into the vehicle and that the people around Vlatko's house would see me, or from any other side, and that they would kill me. I did not have the strength to make up my mind and so I stayed. I had to rely on myself. The tanks left Upper Ahmici. They did not stay in the yard a long time. They returned. But at that time, while the tanks were here, everything was calm. There was no shooting whatsoever during that time. I couldn't hear any firing. When the tank went back to Ahmici and towards the main road and went along to Vitez and came in the vicinity of Pican's cafe, then firing began from all types of weapons, and then it was calm again. So it was a sort of platoon -- a gun blast, and then there was silence again, and nothing else could be heard. No gunfire could be heard after that burst, outburst. I heard the honk of a horn in front of Vlatko Kupreskic's house, and I also heard the siren from Ivica Kupreskic's car, and then the municipal siren could be heard, the fire alarm siren, and at that time, I thought to myself that the emergency warning siren was going on because of the successful action drive to kill and massacre the people in the vicinity of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that while the tanks were there or while you had them in sight, the shooting had stopped. Had you heard any kind of --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Had you heard any kind of shooting or firing before the tanks arrived?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was shooting before that. Until the tanks arrived, shooting could be heard sporadically, but once the tanks got there, silence reigned and no gunfire was heard anywhere. When the tanks returned, as I described earlier on, when they were near Pican's cafe, in my opinion there was a general burst of gunfire from all types of weaponry, and then once again silence reigned. The siren could be heard from Vlatko Kupreskic's house and Ivica Kupreskic's house and the emergency warning siren from the municipality could be heard for the fire brigade in the municipality of Vitez, and what I thought at that moment, that this was probably to celebrate the successful drive of the massacre in the Ahmici region. That is what I think today that it was. It was a celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, after the tanks left, were you able to observe or see anyone that you could recognise?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I can't quite remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Do you recall at what point you left the barn and why you left the barn?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I can't say when I left the barn, at what particular moment I left the barn, but I can say why I left the barn. I did not see but I felt in the barn that something hit, the sound of a hit. I had in the barn two tyres, two tyres belonging to a passenger vehicle at the entrance to the barn, and I heard this tyre hit the ground, and so I thought that somebody was in the barn, so I was even afraid to draw a breath and I couldn't see, but that's what I felt, that somebody was there. I heard some crackling, a crackling noise, and I felt that something had been set alight to. And that was what happened, in fact. I could smell the smell of smoke, and it was the barn crackling, and I had to think quickly what to do because the barn would go up in flames. I tried very slowly, very silently, to creep up and look above the surface of the hay, beyond the hay, to see if there was anybody inside. I did not see anybody. I just even -- above or below the barn, and then I thought, what shall I do next? Shall I go through the barn and then down to take the forks, the hay forks, for manure and so on and then get out that way and to sort of make a hole, burrow a hole through that fertiliser and to mask myself, to camouflage myself with the manure there, with the fertiliser. I had to think quickly. I thought that while I would be doing this and getting out of the barn and downwards, that a soldier would appear, Croatian soldier might appear, so that I felt it safer not to disclose my whereabouts, that there was somebody there. I knew that I could take a log off here from the barn, and I decided to take a log away, a board, a plank, and to place it on the hay but very, very silently, no noise, because I didn't know if anybody was in the barn or out around the barn. I had rubber soles and so on. What I did was I took off one of the planks. I got hold -- I jumped down into the fertiliser, manure, and then I went to this stack of logs here, this log pile, firewood, and this particular stack here (indicating) goes right up towards -- right up one metre up by Sukrija's house, and in that space with the stack of firewood, during the winter when they would take firewood into the house for heating, there was a hole left from the wood they had taken. I sat there, I hid myself there, and there were two parts of -- top parts of vehicles, passenger cars, the hub, and I took away some of the logs so I had -- on three sides I was protected by the logs and the firewood and on one side I was protected by the bonnet of these cars, and that's where I spent the whole day and the whole night, up until about 4.00 in the morning. During that time, if I can continue? Do you want me to continue my story, my recollection of what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, but can I ask a couple of clarification questions first?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you see, once you left the barn, the body of your son Sukrija?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No, I did not. Well -- no, because I went to hide myself amongst the wood, the logs. No, I did not see his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall how long you stayed in the woodpile hiding?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. The whole day. I was there the whole day and the whole night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what your physical condition was during that time period?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I was in a terrible state, it was terrible, because I was all burnt, I had no socks on, I had not much clothing. I was in my pyjamas. It's difficult to describe. I was almost naked. Only in my pyjamas, no socks on my feet. I just had a sort of raincoat to protect myself from the fire and from the heat. That's all I had on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When did you leave the pile, the woodpile?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I left the woodpile in the morning, sometime in the morning on the 17th of April. About 4.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: As you left the woodpile, could you see anything, any bodies?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. When I decided to move and that I couldn't stay in the woodpile any longer, that I couldn't make any presence known and that I had to do this during the night, during the dark. When I left the woodpile, I saw the car of Sukrija, the late Sukrija, in front of his workshop, and his body was lying in front of the car, somewhere here (indicating), in the direction of that tree. That is where the road is. He was lying there near the tree, near the fir tree. When I saw him, I saw that his body was turned over. There was a ditch. I passed by from the front part by his head and tried to take him up and to pull him away so that he could lie straight, but I did not have the strength to do this. I wasn't strong enough to move him, so I left him lying the way he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you mean by not having the strength and tell us how you tried to move him and why it was so difficult for you?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No, I couldn't move him. I wasn't able to. It was difficult because he was lying -- he wasn't lying straight. He was lying on his back. I wanted to turn him over onto his back, but my hands were burnt and I just couldn't do it, so I left him lying there as he was and continued in the direction that I have already described, that I already told you that I went, the direction that I had told myself that I would take, and this took me up to the main road and towards Redzib Ahmic's house. I passed by Redzib Ahmic's and Suad's house. When I found myself there amongst the houses, the cattle smelled me and they knew that somebody was there and they made some noise, and I think that in the barracks, the HVO barracks, they thought that this was just cattle moving about and in front of Andza Kasakic's (phoen) house, the HVO soldiers -- and when I passed through the thicket, I thought that they would fire, but as the cattle moved about throughout the night, this was better for me because they heard the livestock and the cattle and they couldn't hear me passing so I was able to pass through the thicket and emerge towards Caza on the other side. I sat down there; I had no more strength. I sat down to rest a while, and then went on some 20 or 30 metres and had another rest, and once again, I emerged up on the plateau where there was a lot of hay, where the hay was being stacked, and I sat there and thought that I had made it because I had succeeded in emerging from the HVO encirclement. There is a little path linking up the village of Ahmici and Pirici, and I went along that path which took me to the house of my mother. I knocked on the window, and she was there, and I said, "Mother, open the door, but don't turn on the lights." My mother opened the door. I went inside. I sat down on her bed. I asked her, "Could you please light a fire as soon as possible because I'm freezing?" My mother did that; she lit a fire quickly. She made me a cup of tea. I asked her whether she had any cigarettes. She said, yes, she did, and took out a box of cigarettes and some matches and lit a cigarette for me, gave it to me, gave me a glass of tea to drink. I drank the tea, I smoked the cigarette. I don't know whether I drank all the tea or not. And then I heard a burst of gunfire. I just put the glass down on the cupboard. I went towards the window. I heard another burst of fire west of the house, some 250 metres away perhaps, and I went back into the kitchen. My mother heard the firing. "Did you hear the firing?" my mother said, "Yes. You must escape. If they catch you, they'll kill you," she said. She took off her socks from her own feet. I took the sock and put them on one foot and put the sock on my other foot and I left through the door and went up, upwards, and I went up towards Rifet's house, there was nobody there, and I went through the garden towards Barin Gaj, and when I went up onto the plateau in front of Barin Gaj, away from the electricity lines, poles, I stopped and turned to face Ahmici. I turned towards Zume -- the woods. I turned towards Zume, and I saw that everything that was Muslim had been burnt to the ground, and I imagined that everything below that had happened and everything that happened in my own house down there -- I had two brothers, I had a brother-in-law, my daughter, family, relatives, everybody down there; and when I saw that, I saw that there was nothing left, that there was nobody left, and I continued along the road towards Vrhovine upwards, towards Vrhovine, and upon leaving Barin Gaj, I met four or five young men, they entered Barin Gaj. They had rifles. And Vehbija Ahmic and behind them -- Vehbija looked at me and he said, "Is that you, Sakib?" And I said, "Yes, it's me." "What's happening down there?" they asked. I said, "Well, the HVO soldiers came to Pirici and there was a burst of gunfire below my mother's house, another burst of gunfire could be heard some 200, 250 metres away, and you must go to Redzi Grehab (phoen) and one to Gavro's house, Thurma's (phoen) house, and if you can, tell them that -- to stop them, not to go up towards Vrhovine. I continued and reached the village of Vrhovine. There was nobody in the houses. I entered three houses, and there was nobody there. I went to Hadzinica and Blahum (phoen). He was called Kustre. The house was open, and there was nobody in his house either. I went to Esfre Mujezinovic. His house was open too, but there was nobody in the house either. I couldn't go any further. I just could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, let me stop you there for a moment and ask the usher at this time to show the witness the next Prosecution Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 156.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, could you look at the --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you look at this Exhibit 156 and see if you can tell us what that shows. If you have difficulty orienting yourself, just let me know.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you look at the exhibit in front of you on the machine and see if you can tell what that shows.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. It shows the territory around Pirici and Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you see that circle with the 56 next to it?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the circle. I see the little circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Are you having trouble recognising that?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No, no trouble. It's quite a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us, is that your house circled number 56?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Does that white line that zigzags through that map, does that indicate the route that you took when you left Ahmici to your mother's house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, another leading question. The first is: Is the house noted number 56 your house? The second leading question was: Does this route on the map, does it represent your route, the route you took? They are leading questions. The right question would be: What does circle 56 represent, and can you tell us what the line, the white line represents, rather than asking leading questions. This is a little too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, I think it is very clear that the witness had already indicated on this other picture where his house was located and, of course, as for the line, I assume the Prosecutor has made this line on the picture on the basis of what the witness told him before. I don't think it's worth going into minute details. Yes, it is to some extent a leading question, but I would move on. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Barin Gaj in your last narrative. Could you tell us what Barin Gaj is?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Not where it is, but what is it?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: It's a sort of plateau, some high ground from whence you can see the valley of Vitez below, the territory of Ahmici, Santici, and so on; and Barin Gaj, when you say Barin Gaj, it is a forest, in fact, a wood, woodland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What was your physical condition as you stopped at Barin Gaj and overlooked the village of Ahmici? Had you eaten?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No. It was a terrible experience altogether. I was quite lost. I was completely beside myself, and as I say, I was almost 70 per cent killed. When I looked at the territory of Ahmici and everything and when I saw what had happened and what had been done, I was quite beside myself, and that is where I looked down into the valley. From this vantage point here, that's Barin Gaj. That's the plateau, the high ground, and from there, I could view this entire area here, and when I saw everything, I was quite beside myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated Barin Gaj with the pointer. Is there some sort of a letter or marker on this map --

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- that indicates generally where Barin Gaj is? Could you read out the marker or the letter?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: This. Here it is. That's it (indicating). That is my route, the route I took. My house is there; that's the exit to my house. This is between Suad's and Ejeba's (phoen) house. This is the thicket. I came out here onto this clearing. This is the wood. When I got up onto the clearing, I felt that I had managed to escape from the encirclement of the HVO down there. This is the path which links up Pirici and the village of Ahmici, which is over here, and I took this path which led me to my mother's house. That's where my mother's house is located (indicating). This is my neighbour's house, Hazim's, and from there, from my mother's house, I went across -- this is the village of Pirici, all this here (indicating), and I continued via Bace and came to the village of Vidovici, through the garden, and across -- along the path which led to Barin Gaj. This is the path leading straight to Barin Gaj; and when I got here, I went this way (indicating), to this field which gave me a view of everything down below. When I finished all that, and I was completely lost and beside myself, I went back to Vrhovine, up there, and came to the village of Vrhovine; and when I got there, they took me in. A young man -- all the village -- there were no inhabitants in the village because the HVO soldiers shelled Vrhovine and so the women and children left their homes and went up above the village. And when I came, I went out onto the road, and a man came towards me out of the mass that was standing there, the mass of people standing there, he came up to me and said, "Sakib, well, why didn't somebody see to your wounds?" And I said, I told him the truth, I said, "You're the first people that I have encountered because there's no living soul down there in the valley." And he did take out a sort of bandage and bandage one hand and then the other hand, and he said, "We have two more injured people. You're the third. You have a vehicle up by the crossroads, and you will be taken by car, all three of you injured, will be taken to the hospital in Zenica." And that's what happened. The ambulance came, the car came, the vehicle came, and they took us off to Zenica. We went via the Dobriljeno village and then down towards the town, towards-- past Mokosnjice, and a car, an ambulance was waiting for us there and took us over and took us to the hospital where they took us in and where they gave us first aid. Our treatment, our medical treatment was continued there. My entry into hospital took place on the 17th of April, 1993. I left the hospital on the 1st of May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time, and this maybe a good place to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We rise now. Thirty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, we left off with your having been taken to the hospital. What city was this in that you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: The town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And again, will you tell us how long you were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I was admitted to hospital on the 17th of April, 1993, and I left the hospital on the 1st of May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Are you aware of some inaccuracy in your release date as noted in a report?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There is an inaccuracy. They said that I had been discharged on the 26th, according to their date. And there's a difference also in the month, there's a small error. Yes, there is an inaccuracy, but minor inaccuracy. It's a difference of a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you remain in the same hospital for that whole period of time or were you transferred from one hospital to another?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in the same hospital all that time. I was moved from the main hospital to the medical school, as there were a large number of wounded arriving and all the beds were occupied. There were people lying in the corridors. And so as to free some beds for the heavily wounded, those who had recovered to some extent were transferred to the medical school where their treatment was continued in the same way as in the hospital. We continued to receive the same therapy, X-rays, check-ups of the heart function, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe, to the best your recollection, the kind of treatment that you received when you arrived at the main hospital in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the question. Immediately I was given first-aid treatment, and then treatment was continued in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did they treat your burn wounds?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: They treated them with some lotions, creams, sprays.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you receive any medication, any pills?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. We were given pills, and shots and all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you describe whether you were in any pain at this time and tell us how severe that pain was?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I felt very strong pain at the very beginning when they were giving me first-aid. I think the pain was worse than while I was actually burning. The pain was bad. My heart was examined many times. I was under constant medical control regarding the heart function. I was never left unattended by a nurse in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How long did the pain last?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: For a long time. I had pain -- I felt pain for almost three or four months. The treatment was slow. It took time to heal. I had terrible problems with these burns and wounds. My fingers were totally stiff. I couldn't move any of them. All this is new skin. I had lost all my nails from my fingers. There was a shortage of medicines too. I had a friend in the town of Zenica who managed to find special lily oil which I used to massage my fingers, except for this finger, which remains stiff. I don't have any strength in that finger. You see, the finger remains fixed. There is no strength in it. As for the rest of my fingers, they're working well now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What about your face? Was that also injured, and if so, what did they do to treat that?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: My face was terrible. It was also badly burned and scorched. It was treated in the same way, with sprays. When I say "sprays," these were to fill in the gaps so as to prevent infection. But the pain was very bad. It is hard to describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: While you were in the hospital at this time period, do you recall giving two statements to investigators?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you tell those investigators everything you knew about what had happened in your house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What didn't you tell them?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: What I didn't tell them or why I didn't tell them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What you didn't tell them.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: First of all, in that statement I didn't dare name the killers of my children. I didn't dare name Zoran Kupreskic, I didn't dare name Mirjan Kupreskic in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Why didn't you dare name the killers of your children?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I didn't dare name them because the war was in full swing in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I couldn't know at the time how the war would end and how it would come to a stop, and that is the reason why I didn't have the courage to name anyone at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, in later statements you did name Zoran and Mirjan as the killers of your children and your family. Why did you do it in later statements? What had happened?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I came to a decision in my thoughts, and I said to myself, why? Why should I protect the people who killed my dearest ones, when they had the strength to carry out this massacre, these murders, these evil things they did? Who should I fear to tell the truth? I'm not afraid of anyone any more. And I shall never be afraid of anyone any more. All those who did that, let them look after -- let them fear me. They are the criminals and not me. That is one reason. And secondly, I always want the truth. I always want to tell the truth. Each individual, each person on this earth, my opinion that whatever he does, he should suffer the consequences. If I work in a company for a month, the company is obliged to pay me for the labour I have invested in that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, at this time I would like to show you a brief video and show the Court a brief video, and as we look at it, it's a short one, and after it's played I would like you to comment on it, please. With the permission of the court, I would at this time ask for the video to be played. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Radovic is asking--

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would be grateful to the Prosecutor if he could tell us when this tape was taken and where it was shown, because this was obviously for a TV programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I will ask the witness if he recalls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, was that you on the tape?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall where that interview took place?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: In Zenica, in the hospital at Crkvice. I think this took place on the 18th or the 19th of April, I'm not quite sure. But it was with -- one of those two days, right after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: One further question. Which TV company shot this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know which TV company shot this? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I think it was Radio Zenica. Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, we could see from that tape that -- we could see from that tape that there was some injuries. Could you tell us if you can recall how you were feeling on the day you gave that tape -- that taped interview?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I was in a very bad condition. I was not feeling well at all. It is hard to describe. I was still beside myself. I felt lost. I had lost everything. And to this day I feel awful. I was sick. I was in a shock, in a state of shock for days, because I had lost all that was dear to me. You can imagine how I could have felt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, sorry to interrupt you. I imagine you're going to provide the Court with a transcript of that videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, we will, and we have transcripts prepared. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: It may be, Your Honour, that these transcripts have already been provided to the Court as well as to Defence counsel, but we are happy to provide another set of copies. In any event, we are prepared to provide copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At the time you made this videotape, Mr. Ahmic, had you yet decided to come forward and reveal the killers of your family?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: At that time, at the time that this was filmed, I don't know what I had in mind. At the time I certainly was undecided whether to name those people or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think you indicated earlier that there was a war going on. At the time that the war was going on, did you know who was going to win that war?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you in the Zenica hospital when the city of Zenica was shelled?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At the time you gave this interview, did you know where your family members were?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I didn't know. I didn't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you come to find out what had happened to the bodies of your family members in that house?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was informed about it. They came to the hospital, and they told me about all these killed members of my family in the house, that for each person a coffin had been provided, a Muslim priest, a Hajra, for the religious burial rights. They wanted to hear what my wish was regarding where they should be buried, my children. I told them we have two cemeteries in the area of Ahmici, which were inaccessible at the time, both of them, so I asked them to check and see whether it was possible in Stari Vitez, and if possible, in Stari Vitez, they should be buried there. And if that was not possible, if not in Stari Vitez, if it was impossible to reach it, then I asked them to bring them to Zenica. And if they were to be buried in Zenica, that they should come for me so that I should be present at the time my children were buried. However, nobody came back again. I heard that they had been buried in Stari Vitez, and that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the person you were talking to about the bodies of your family?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I think it was Thomas, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you can recall, the number of your house as it was numbered in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. It was number 5. Number 5 was the number of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. Usher, I would ask the witness be shown this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 158. The videotape has been marked 157.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, could you please look at the Exhibit 158 and identify that, please?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: This is my son Naser. Please, don't mind me. Please don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Perhaps we should take a brief recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Those are my eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, the Court considers that it is not necessary to show the witness all those pictures. The fact that his relatives were killed is not in dispute. Defence counsel, I imagine, will not dispute that, and I don't see why he should go through a most excruciating, terrible experience. So I wonder whether we could move on to other matters? (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: He indicated to me, Mr. President, that he wanted that opportunity to show his son. We have no other pictures of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, are you now capable of proceeding just a little while longer?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I only have just two or three questions now, and they're also difficult questions.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you please look around the courtroom and see if you can identify Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Zoran Kupreskic is to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is he in the front row or the next row behind it?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: In the front row.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May the record reflect he's identified Zoran Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you look around the room and see if you can identify Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Mirjan Kupreskic is next to Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May the record reflect he's identified Mirjan Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were these the two men who were in your house on April 16, 1993, while your family was killed before your eyes?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you may sit. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you also look around the room and identify Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And where is he sitting, please?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: To the left, left of Zoran and Mirjan is Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell me what colour of clothing he is wearing?

utterances.speaker: Sakib Ahmic
utterances.text: Vlatko is wearing a white shirt and a dark tie, a blue tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May the record reflect that he has identified Vlatko Kupreskic. Your Honours, I have no more questions except to formally offer the exhibits that we have entered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits from 150 to 158.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Those exhibits. I note that there is time left in the day; however, I wonder if, after this exhausting experience, Mr. Ahmic is willing or capable to begin cross-examination today, a process that undoubtedly will not finish today in any event, and he needs to come back the week after next. I think he is quite exhausted, but perhaps the Court can question him to see if he is able to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Moskowitz. First of all, let me turn to counsel for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic to ask them whether they would like to start cross-examining the witness today. Mr. Radovic, you say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because when we first learned that Mr. Sakib Ahmic was going to substitute for the witness who was supposed to be testifying, you yourself stated, and we also were made to believe, that he was not going to be cross-examined, so we would like to keep it that way. Let me just add something else, if I may? I see that we have had identification of the accused here, but we believe that it, as a rule, is done when the witness knows the accused. In this case, it is not -- it is not -- there is no controversy there because they were neighbours, so I see no particular point in having this witness identify the accused who were his neighbours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The point is not that he identified them as neighbours but as persons whom he claims saw killing his relatives, so it is a different point. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The dearest people to my heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you intend to go on with the proceedings and if the witness is able and is willing to accept cross-examination, our colleague Krajina may have one or two relatively easy questions for him, and if the witness is agreeable, I would then turn the floor over to my colleague, Mr. Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Pavkovic. Let me turn to Mr. Ahmic and ask him: Mr. Ahmic, do you want to stop now and go back home because you are exhausted, or do you want us to continue, and in this case, counsel for one of the accused will ask you questions. If you feel tired, you are entitled to withdraw now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest and frank with you, I am not just exhausted, I am really exhausted, and I don't think that I have the strength to continue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So you may leave the courtroom now and we will continue with procedural matters. You will come back when we resume our --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too and good-bye. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us discuss a few matters relating to some matters of relevance to our proceedings. First of all, the question of Witness number 6, the lady we mentioned this morning. Now, our position is that we will request the physicians here in The Hague to provide us with further medical reports after the check-up, and we understand you have probably seen the report which was circulated this afternoon. The check-up was at lunch time. I assume probably by Monday we will receive a detailed report from the doctors. Meanwhile, she will be allowed to leave. I understand she is very keen to go back to her house. In light of the report, we will decide what to do, but our intention is that she should be called back and give evidence in court. We are acting under Rule 89 -- sorry. I think 98, it must be. Yes, 98, to be read in conjunction with Rule 89, and on the strength of those Rules, we intend to call back the witness. We will take all the necessary steps short of, of course, forcing the witness to come back to The Hague. If, as I hope, she is better, she will be given, at our request, psychological support, she should be treated while at home, if possible, and when she comes back, I hope that the Witness and Victims Unit will provide psychological support to her while she will be in The Hague, and I think that she should testify, say, one or two days, at the latest, after her return to The Hague, because we understand from the persons working for the Victims and Witnesses Unit that for the witnesses spending a few days here, a lot of time here, is quite taxing and they become exhausted and, of course, also this becomes very difficult. So as soon as she gets here, as soon as possible she should be called to testify. But, as I say, we will let you know. We are taking this matter in hand. As for the other witnesses, I wonder whether the Prosecution could provide both the Court and the Defence with a list of the witnesses to be heard as soon as we resume our proceedings, a list and the order, and also I wonder whether the Prosecution at this stage can give a rough idea of the number, the total number of witnesses they intend to call so that we can make plans to see whether we may finish by mid-October, as we hope. In this connection, we feel now that we have to go back to our old timetable. We can't afford to, in a way, work for about four hours fifteen minutes? No, we have to go back to the old schedule whereby we spend about, I think, five hours, working hours, per day, so we propose that when we resume our proceedings on the 15th of September, we will sit from 9.30 to 12.30 and again from 2.00 to 5.00. So longer hours. Friday afternoons will be off, but at some stage, if need be, we may have to go back to longer hours as we have done yesterday and today. But let us avoid that because it is, of course, difficult and awkward for everybody. I wonder whether the Prosecutor has some information to provide at this stage? Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, regarding the first question, regarding the order of appearance of witnesses for the week beginning the 15th of September, we have prepared the names of witnesses, and I think that in view of the fact that the cross-examination of Mr. Sakib Ahmic will certainly take several hours of hearing, we have to review this order of appearance of witnesses, and perhaps, at the beginning of next week, we can fax to the Defence and the Court a list of witnesses that will be properly corrected. As for the continuation of our proceedings, right through until the month of October, we intend to consult on these three weeks of hearings and prepare for them, and I think that we will provide to your Court an overview of the number of witnesses. I wish just to say that our considerations are the same as yours, that is, that we will do our best to present the evidence within the time period required by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: When do you think you could give us a transcript of the videotape? Is it ready? Probably. It is ready. So if we could get it even this afternoon? Yes. Thank you. Well, I owe an apology to the Prosecution, actually, now that I have got it, I realise, somewhere in my file. This document was already to be found and actually it had already been given to the Court, and I imagine the Defence as well has got an original transcript in Croatian. Any matter? I wonder whether the Defence wish -- oh, yes, Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: A question, a legal question. We envisage the week from the 15th to the 18th of September to call as witnesses police officers, Dutch police officers, who accompanied us in Bosnia for some of our examinations on the spot, and the Court has at its disposal the reports submitted by these police officers. We are calling them, let that be clear, as witnesses of fact, and therefore, they will be subject to cross-examination. We have disclosed to the Defence their names and the area, the substance of their testimony in August 1998. That is in line with the order that you gave. I think three or four days are lacking, but I wonder whether, in accordance with Rule, I think it is 127, you can allow this reduction of the time required? We are not even quite sure that they will be able to testify next week because of other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the videotape which we viewed today, we have an objection. This videotape, in fact, shows an excerpt from the interview of Sakib Ahmic with either the journalist or whoever filmed this. When videotapes are used, we cannot be sure whether this videotape contains everything that Sakib Ahmic said during this television programme. We have certain information regarding this broadcast, and we ourselves attempted to get a copy of it, but we see that the Prosecution was able to do so. We would like you to advise the Prosecution to show us the entire videotape containing the interview with Sakib Ahmic so that we can see whether the excerpt that we have seen contains everything that he had stated in the hospital or whether this was just an excerpt which would tend to support the case that the Prosecution is trying to offer. We believe that there may be other elements in there, and I don't think that we need to go into detail about that now here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radovic, I think your request is quite reasonable, and I wonder whether the Prosecutor -- I see Mr. Moskowitz. Could you provide the whole text -- the whole videotape?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm not aware that there is another one in our possession, but I will undertake another search to see if there's a longer videotape somewhere in the building, but it's my understanding that this is the videotape that we have and that there is not another one. There are other witnesses who are on the videotape being interviewed in what we have. I'm not aware, however, that we have a longer one of Mr. Ahmic. But we will look again and see if we can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Also because we understand from the witness that it was made by the Zenica TV. Probably you could ask the company in Zenica to provide you a copy of the full tape, the whole interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Because I think that Mr. Radovic is absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: However, Mr. Terrier had raised the issue of the -- what we felt were expert witnesses, but the Prosecution would like to call those police officers as fact witnesses, I understand. I wonder whether the Defence are ready to waive their right of having 30 days? It is the new Rule which we adopted about the expert witnesses. Do you remember the number of the -- I don't have it here. Thirty days. I remember there was 30 days. If you don't waive this right, I mean, the witness could be called a bit later, but really ... Mr. Pavkovic, are you able to set out your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me, Mr. President, that the Defence would be agreeable that these expert witnesses be heard within a time frame; in other words, we do not need 30 days' notice on the names of these witnesses and their statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Also because I think Rule 94 bis actually does not apply because you don't intend to call them as expert witnesses. They are fact witnesses, so the normal rules on the disclosure of their statements apply, and I wonder whether, under those Rules, the necessary time limit is met.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Quite, Mr. President. The list that I am referring to, this guideline envisages 30 days, but this has not elapsed, only 25 or 26 or 27 days have elapsed. That is the only problem that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding, Mr. Pavkovic, that you will not object to the calling of those witnesses by the Prosecution two or three days before the expiry of the delay time limit of 30 days?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. We do not object that these witnesses be called and their testimony be heard within this time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other matter? Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just briefly. I would like to make the record absolutely clear with regard to this videotape. The videotape that we played today was shown to Defence counsel I think a week ago Friday and they were fully aware of the videotape that we had in our possession, and we have not heard, until this very moment, that they are aware of another longer videotape, so I am, first of all, a little bit surprised that this was not raised sooner, and had it been raised sooner, we would have done the search, and if we had found a longer videotape, we would have played it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but they have a right to raise objections at any time, and probably after seeing the videotape, they realise that this might be just a little bit of the whole videotape. Probably the interview with the witness was much longer, and they're entitled to see whether or not it was longer. So whether or not they were right in raising this issue today, I think they are right to do so, and therefore, let us check. I mean, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: To check, in particular, in Zenica. I wonder whether you could ask them to be careful and to send you the -- if not the original -- ideally, we should get the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I will speak to the investigator this afternoon about that very matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, the original. If we could get the original, if not, a copy certified by the relevant people in Zenica, and if possible, the whole interview. Thank you. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, there was this TV organisation called ZETEL. Apparently now it has become part of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Television organisation. So maybe this search may not now be limited to Zenica alone but maybe to Sarajevo as well. We would like if the entire programme would be shown here for the Tribunal so that this would save us calling several witnesses who have seen the entire programme and have been aware of it for some time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I intended, what I had in mind, namely, to try to have the videotape with the whole programme, and I agree with Mr. Radovic, probably since now the original copy of that videotape might be in Sarajevo, I wonder whether the Prosecution could carry out research, undertake some sort of research even there, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I will ask the investigator to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there other matters? If there are no other matters, before rising, I would like to take this opportunity to thank the interpreters. You probably don't know that the interpreters who, as we all know, are excellent, and they yesterday came to see me to ask whether they could have longer breaks because they normally work for an hour and a half and then there is a break, and I insisted, "No, we have to work for two hours without any break," and they accepted, they were extremely friendly and kind, and I would like to thank them most warmly for being so understanding. There are no other matters, so we will now adjourn until Tuesday -- I think it's Tuesday, 15th of September, 9.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 5.08 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of September, 1998, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
